extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent prosecutors, and patent examiners (those dealing with 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter eligibility issues)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practice tips for drafting claims, specifications, and responses to avoid or rebut 35 U.S.C. §101 rejections (Alice/Mayo framework), with examples from Federal Circuit decisions. Focuses on software, data-processing, measurement, and other technology areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attack the identification of the abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Attack the identification of the abstract idea: As instructed in the May 4, 2016 Memorandum at page 3: Examiners should be familiar with any cited decision relied upon in making or maintaining a rejection to ensure that the rejection is reasonably tied to the facts of the case and to avoid relying upon language taken out of context. Examiners should not go beyond those concepts that are similar to what the courts have identified as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge the examiner's characterization of the claims; show the cited cases are not reasonably tied to the facts of the application and that language was taken out of context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Enfish, McRo, and Berkheimer memos/analogs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the McRo, Enfish, and Berkheimer memos
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame arguments using these precedents/memos: emphasize claim elements that show improvements in computer technology (Enfish), that create technical solutions to technical problems (McRo), and factual disputes about conventionality (Berkheimer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue a technical solution to a technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue a technical solution to a technical problem, clearly identifying why the problem and the solution are technical in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly identify the technical problem being solved and explain how the claimed features provide a technical solution (not merely a business/abstract one). Demonstrate how elements improve computing or other technological functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recite and emphasize generation of new information
rubrics_metrics.description: Recite and emphasize generation of new information that did not previously exist, which sets up an analogy to Enfish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the claims produce or derive new data/metrics/information (not merely reorganize or present known information) to support eligibility analogies to cases like Enfish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recite and emphasize user interactivity that improves data presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recite and emphasize user interactivity that improves data presentation, which sets up an analogy to Core Wireless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize interactive presentation features and how they improve user-device interaction or data presentation beyond abstract displaying of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point to a particular inventive technological process
rubrics_metrics.description: Point to a particular inventive technological process to distinguish from Electric Power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish your claims from Electric Power by identifying a particular tool, process, or technological mechanism that is inventive rather than merely collecting/analyzing/displaying information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid characterization as merely 'collecting, analyzing, and displaying' information
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that the claims have been over simplified and improperly characterized broadly as 'collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying certain results of the collection and analysis' in an attempt to compare the claims to Electric Power Group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate concrete claim elements beyond the caricature; show the combination of limitations as a whole provide technical improvements or specific inventive technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not merely presenting results of collection and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: "merely presenting the results of abstract processes of collecting and analyzing information, without more (such as identifying a particular tool for presentation), is abstract as an ancillary part of such collection and analysis."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include claim elements that identify specific presentation tools or techniques (not generic 'displaying') to avoid being characterized as mere presentation of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) is unreasonable if overbroad
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadest reasonable interpretation: Argue that the interpretation of the claims is unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the examiner's characterization stretches claim language beyond reasonable meaning, argue against that BRI to prevent over-generalization to abstract concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify claimed improvement to computer-related technology (Enfish guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the improvement offered by the claimed invention and inquire whether that improvement represents a specific improvement to the technology itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how the claim's 'character as a whole' is directed to technological improvement (example: Enfish's self-referential table improving database operation). Describe concrete technical benefits and how they differ from routine computing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support unconventional measurement/algorithm with specification and facts (Exergen guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim employs a natural law, if the measurement method is not conventional, routine, and well-understood, it can supply an inventive concept under Alice/Mayo step two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include in the specification mathematical equations, derivations, experimental results, and factual support showing the method is unconventional and not routine. Assert and support factual findings (per Berkheimer) where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do more than provide notification (FairWarning/Classen guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider making sure your claims do something with the information that is collected beyond merely providing a notice that an event has occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modify claims to act on the detected condition or include steps that effectuate change (not just alerting) to improve chances of eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim specific steps and new data structures, not just results (Finjan guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating a new data structure based on conventional activity (virus scanning) can satisfy the Alice test provided your claims recite more than just the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include specific steps that accomplish the result and clear description in the specification so that claim construction supports a narrower, technology-improving reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wholly functional/generic claim language (Glasswall guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims framed in wholly functional terms without how the invention performs the functions are vulnerable; the court found claims similar to Intellectual Ventures I (Symantec) which 'simply require generic computer-implemented steps.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recite how the computer receives files, determines types, parses content, extracts allowable data, creates substitutes, and authorizes forward — show concrete mechanisms and improvements in computer functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show claimed improvement to a specific platform or computer technology (Downing guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike in McRo and DDR Holdings, the claims did not include an improvement and did not claim an improvement in Excel spreadsheets or an improved resource planning computer technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claiming an implementation on a platform (e.g., Excel), include improvements to that platform or claim features that change how the platform operates rather than simply running an idea on a known platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claiming mathematical concepts, claim improvement to technology (Gitlin guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners need to claim an improvement to a computer or some other technology when claiming a mathematical algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not claim pure mathematical interpolation/algorithm alone; tether the algorithm to a technological improvement or specific implementation that changes operation of a device or system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming fundamental economic practices (Villena guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to fundamental economic practices long prevalent in commerce (e.g., property valuation) are abstract under Alice step one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drafting claims that recite longstanding commercial practices; instead, add technological features or inventive concepts that transform the abstract economic practice into a technological application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim physical/tangible form or data that acts on something (Wang guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: For categories other than process, the eligible subject matter must exist in some physical or tangible form. What is claimed (e.g., a phonetic symbol system) that is not a 'concrete thing' or 'tangible article' may fail §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider claiming data stored on a non-transitory medium or claim that the data acts on or controls a physical device; avoid claims that are merely printed matter or pure definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid result-oriented display claims lacking technical detail (Interval Licensing guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract idea was found because the claims were result oriented, without technical detail. The abstract idea was 'displaying a second set of data without interfering with a first set of data.' At step 2, the claims were found to not recite a technical solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include technical details about how the display is implemented, scheduling, acquisition, update, and specific mechanisms rather than high-level result-oriented language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft claims with concrete technical elements (example: dynamic stability metrics claim features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite technical elements such as frequency instability, voltages, power flows, phase angles, damping, oscillation modes, derived from phasor measurements, displaying event analysis results in visuals/tables/charts, concurrent visualization of measurements and dynamic stability metrics, real-time accumulation and updating of measurements, and deriving a composite indicator of reliability that uses real time measurements and non-grid data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, include concrete sensor/measurement sources, derived metrics, real-time processing, visualization modalities, and how those elements combine technically to produce a new capability (e.g., power grid vulnerability indicator) rather than high-level data collection/display descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide detailed specification support and factual evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Exergen and related entries stress that factual findings and specification support (e.g., mathematical equations, experimental testing/results) can be decisive in showing claims are not conventional or routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Populate the specification with equations, derivations, test data, descriptions of unconventional steps, implementation details, and any empirical evidence to support non-conventionality and enable meaningful claim construction and rebuttal of examiner assertions.
